items.prompt: Why does the brain cycle repeatedly between light sleep, deep sleep and dream-filled sleep through a single night?

options.label: The brain alternates between distinct stages that each do a different kind of work
options.feedback: Each stage of sleep runs its own pattern of brain activity, tuned to a different job, and the brain moves through them in a repeating sequence.

options.label: It's a single unbroken state that only looks different from the outside
options.feedback: The stages differ inside the brain itself, in electrical activity and in what's happening to the body, not just in outward appearance.

options.label: The brain shuts off entirely between light sleep and deep sleep
options.feedback: The brain doesn't switch off at any point during the night; it stays active throughout, just in different patterns.

options.label: Cycling between stages is a random, meaningless side effect
options.feedback: The stages recur in a fairly consistent order and each one is linked to distinct kinds of brain activity, not to randomness.

items.ok_line: Different stages, each doing its own kind of work.
items.ko_line: Ask what actually changes inside the brain from one stage to the next.
items.exp_text: Sleep isn't one uniform state; it's built from several stages, each marked by its own pattern of brain activity, muscle tone and eye movement. The brain moves through these stages in a fairly regular sequence over the course of the night, cycling back through them repeatedly rather than settling into just one. Each pass through the cycle gives every stage another turn at the particular job it does.

items.prompt: What is the brain doing during the deepest stage of sleep, when brain waves slow down and become synchronised?

options.label: Running restorative processes such as tissue repair and clearing built-up waste
options.feedback: Slow, synchronised brain activity coincides with the body's repair and clean-up work being at its most active.

options.label: Processing the day's visual images into vivid dream stories
options.feedback: Vivid dream storytelling is linked to a different stage, one where brain activity looks much more like being awake, not this slow synchronised one.

options.label: Practising the muscle movements used earlier that day
options.feedback: Muscles are kept largely quiet during this stage rather than being exercised.

options.label: Scanning the surroundings for danger more closely than while awake
options.feedback: Awareness of the surroundings is reduced during this stage, not heightened; that isn't what the slow, synchronised activity is doing.

items.ok_line: The body's repair shift, running while the brain idles low.
items.ko_line: Think about what the body catches up on when brain activity slows and synchronises.
items.exp_title: The slow stage is the repair shift
items.exp_text: When brain waves slow and synchronise across large areas, the brain has shifted into a low-activity pattern that frees up the body for maintenance work: tissues repair themselves, and fluid movement through the brain steps up to help clear out waste that built up during the day. Growth-related processes also run more heavily during this stage than at any other point in the cycle. It is, in effect, the stage where the body gets its housekeeping done.

items.prompt: Why is the sleep stage where the eyes dart rapidly back and forth also the stage where the most vivid dreaming happens?

options.label: The brain becomes highly active in this stage, resembling wakeful activity far more than the deep, slow stage does
options.feedback: Brain activity during this stage looks much closer to being awake, driving the busy, story-like activity that dreaming needs.

options.label: The eyes are what generate dreams, and their movement causes the images
options.feedback: Eye movement doesn't create the dream content; it's a side effect of the brain's heightened activity during this stage, not the cause of it.

options.label: This stage is when the brain is at its quietest
options.feedback: The opposite is true: this stage is one of the most electrically active periods of the whole night, not the quietest.

options.label: The muscles are working hardest during this stage, which produces the dream
options.feedback: The muscles are actually kept unusually still during this stage; it's brain activity, not muscle effort, that drives the dreaming.

items.ok_line: A brain running busy, almost as if awake.
items.ko_line: Compare how active the brain is in this stage with how active it is in deep, slow-wave sleep.
items.exp_title: A brain running as if awake
items.exp_text: During this stage the brain's electrical activity picks up sharply, taking on a fast, irregular pattern much closer to being awake than to the slow waves of deep sleep. Regions tied to vision, emotion and memory switch on strongly, generating the vivid, story-like scenes that make up a dream. The rapid eye movement that gives this stage its name is simply a visible sign of just how busy the brain has become underneath.

items.prompt: Why do the arms and legs go essentially limp during the most vivid dreaming stage of sleep?

options.label: The brainstem actively blocks the signals that would otherwise move the muscles
options.feedback: A deliberate block on outgoing movement signals stops the body from physically acting out whatever is happening in the dream.

options.label: The muscles are simply too exhausted from the day to move
options.feedback: Ordinary tiredness isn't the cause. The stillness is an active block from the brainstem, not fatigue.

options.label: The nerves connecting brain to muscle are temporarily disconnected
options.feedback: The connection stays intact; what happens is that signals along it are actively suppressed rather than the wiring being broken.

options.label: Blood stops flowing to the limbs during this stage
options.feedback: Blood flow to the limbs continues as normal; it's the movement signal that is blocked, not the blood supply.

items.ok_line: A deliberate block, not exhaustion or disconnection.
items.ko_line: Ask whether the stillness is a side effect or something the brain is doing on purpose.
items.exp_title: A deliberate lock on the muscles
items.exp_text: While the brain is generating vivid dream activity, a part of the brainstem sends out signals that actively suppress the pathways carrying movement commands down to the muscles. That suppression keeps the arms and legs essentially limp no matter how much running, climbing or fighting is happening in the dream. It's a protective lock that keeps a sleeping body from acting out whatever the dreaming brain is imagining.

items.prompt: Why does fluid flow through brain tissue increase noticeably during sleep?

options.label: It flushes out waste products that built up in brain tissue during waking hours
options.feedback: A stepped-up flow of fluid rinses metabolic byproducts out from between brain cells, clearing them away.

options.label: It delivers extra oxygen that the brain doesn't need while awake
options.feedback: Oxygen delivery isn't the change here; the boosted flow is about clearing waste, not supplying extra fuel.

options.label: It cools the brain down after a day of heavy thinking
options.feedback: Cooling isn't the purpose of this fluid surge; it's driven by waste clearance, not by temperature.

options.label: It carries new memories from short-term to long-term storage directly through the fluid
options.feedback: Memory consolidation happens through neural circuits replaying activity, not by anything being physically carried in this fluid.

items.ok_line: A rinse cycle for the brain's own tissue.
items.ko_line: Think about what accumulates in brain tissue over a day of activity, and what needs removing.
items.exp_text: Brain cells produce waste byproducts as they work, the same way any busy tissue does, and those byproducts build up in the narrow spaces between cells over the course of a waking day. During sleep, the channels that fluid moves through around brain cells widen, and the flow through those channels picks up noticeably, flushing the accumulated waste out and away. The brain effectively runs a rinse cycle on its own tissue while the rest of it is occupied with sleep's other stages.

items.prompt: Why do dreams so often feel bizarre and disconnected, jumping from scene to scene without logic?

options.label: The brain regions responsible for logical checking and self-control are much less active during vivid dreaming
options.feedback: With those checking regions quieter, strange or impossible scenes pass by without the usual challenge of 'does this make sense'.

options.label: The eyes are sending confused signals to the brain during this stage
options.feedback: The eyes aren't receiving outside images at all during sleep; the confusion comes from inside the brain's own activity, not from eye input.

options.label: Dreams are edited afterward by memory into a strange order
options.feedback: The strangeness is happening as the dream unfolds, driven by which brain regions are active at the time, not added afterward by memory.

options.label: The parts of the brain that handle logic are actually working harder than usual
options.feedback: Those logic-checking regions are quieter during this stage, not more active, which is exactly why the odd scenes go unchallenged.

items.ok_line: The internal fact-checker is off duty.
items.ko_line: Think about which part of the brain would normally flag a scene as impossible, and what it's doing right now.
items.exp_text: The region at the front of the brain that normally checks whether a situation makes sense and keeps behaviour under control becomes markedly less active during vivid dreaming, while regions handling emotion and vivid imagery stay busy. With that checking function turned down, scenes can shift abruptly and impossible events can pass by unchallenged, because nothing is flagging them as wrong. The dream feels bizarre precisely because the part of the brain that would normally object has gone quiet.

items.prompt: Why do most dreams slip away within minutes of waking, even ones that felt vivid at the time?

options.label: The brain regions needed to lay down a lasting memory are themselves subdued during the dreaming stage
options.feedback: Without those memory-forming regions fully engaged during the dream, there's little lasting trace left for the waking brain to retrieve.

options.label: Dreams are too short to be remembered
options.feedback: Length isn't the issue; dreaming stretches can last a while. The trouble is that memory-forming regions weren't fully engaged to record it.

options.label: The brain deliberately erases every dream the moment a person wakes
options.feedback: There's no active erasing step at waking. The memory was simply never encoded very strongly to begin with.

options.label: Dreams are stored permanently but the brain loses the ability to access them
options.feedback: It isn't a case of a strong memory becoming unreachable; the trace itself was weak from the start, since encoding regions were subdued.

items.ok_line: Encoded weakly to begin with, so there's little to hold onto.
items.ko_line: Ask how strongly the dream was ever recorded in the first place, rather than what happens after waking.
items.exp_title: Never strongly recorded in the first place
items.exp_text: Laying down a memory that lasts normally depends on certain regions near the middle of the brain working together with the rest of the cortex, and during vivid dreaming those memory-forming regions run at reduced activity compared with waking life. A dream can feel intensely vivid as it happens without ever being encoded strongly enough to leave a lasting trace behind. Whatever fragment does get caught tends to survive only if it's replayed in the mind right at the moment of waking, before it can fade.

items.prompt: How might a night of vivid dreaming help someone stumble onto an unusual solution to a problem?

options.label: The brain forms looser, more unusual connections between unrelated memories during this stage
options.feedback: With its normal, cautious associations relaxed, the brain can link ideas that waking thought would keep firmly apart.

options.label: The brain solves problems logically, step by step, while dreaming
options.feedback: Dreaming activity is loose and associative rather than step-by-step logical; that's actually why unusual, unexpected links can appear.

options.label: Dreaming has nothing to do with how ideas get connected
options.feedback: Dreaming activity specifically favours unusual, loosely linked connections between memories, which is exactly the mechanism behind this effect.

options.label: The brain simply replays the problem exactly as it was left the night before
options.feedback: A plain, unchanged replay wouldn't produce anything new; what helps is the loosened, unusual linking that happens during this stage, not an exact repeat.

items.ok_line: Unrelated memories, linked in ways waking thought wouldn't allow.
items.ko_line: Think about how tightly or loosely the brain links ideas together during this particular stage.
items.exp_text: During vivid dreaming, the regions that store memories become highly active while the region that normally keeps associations tightly disciplined runs quieter than usual. With that discipline relaxed, memories that waking thought would keep filed separately can brush against each other and combine in ways that hadn't occurred before. A problem left unsolved the night before can come out the other side connected to some distant memory that supplies an angle nobody had tried while awake.

items.prompt: Why does staying awake for many hours in a row make it harder and harder to concentrate?

options.label: A chemical byproduct of neural activity builds up in the brain the longer a person stays awake
options.feedback: That byproduct steadily accumulates the longer neurons keep firing, and its buildup is what drags concentration down.

options.label: The brain simply runs out of oxygen after being awake too long
options.feedback: Oxygen supply to the brain doesn't run low from being awake for a long stretch; the trouble comes from a build-up of a different chemical byproduct.

options.label: Muscles get tired first, and tired muscles make the brain feel tired too
options.feedback: The drop in concentration is a brain-level change tied to a chemical build-up, not something borrowed from tired muscles.

options.label: The eyes stop working properly after long hours awake, which is mistaken for poor concentration
options.feedback: The eyes keep functioning normally; the concentration problem originates in the brain's own chemistry, not in vision.

items.ok_line: A byproduct that piles up the longer the brain stays on.
items.ko_line: Think about what accumulates in the brain simply from staying awake and active, hour after hour.
items.exp_title: A byproduct that piles up with wakefulness
items.exp_text: Every time a neuron fires, it leaves behind a small amount of a byproduct that then lingers in the fluid around brain cells, and each additional hour awake adds more of it on top of what's already there. As that byproduct accumulates, it interferes with the signalling that keeps attention sharp, making concentration progressively harder to hold onto. Sleep clears that byproduct back down, which is part of why concentration returns once a person has slept.

items.prompt: Why can someone get up, walk around and even carry out simple actions while still fully asleep, as happens in sleepwalking?

options.label: The brain regions controlling movement wake partly while the regions for conscious awareness stay in deep sleep
options.feedback: That mismatch lets the body carry out movements while the part of the brain that would normally be aware of doing them stays offline.

options.label: Sleepwalking happens during the most vivid dreaming stage, so the person is acting out a dream
options.feedback: Sleepwalking actually happens during deep, slow-wave sleep, a stage where the body isn't normally locked still the way it is during vivid dreaming.

options.label: The person is briefly and fully awake without remembering it afterward
options.feedback: A sleepwalker isn't fully awake at the time; the regions responsible for conscious awareness remain in a deep-sleep state throughout.

options.label: Sleepwalking is caused by dreaming so intensely that the body is forced to move
options.feedback: The movement isn't driven by dream content at all; it comes from a partial waking of movement-control regions while awareness stays asleep.

items.ok_line: The body stirs while awareness stays behind, still asleep.
items.ko_line: Ask which parts of the brain would need to wake up for someone to walk, and which would need to stay asleep for them not to notice.
items.exp_title: Two systems, out of step with each other
items.exp_text: Deep sleep normally keeps both movement and awareness offline together, but occasionally the circuits that control basic movement rouse to a partly active state while the circuits responsible for conscious awareness remain deeply asleep. That mismatch lets the body sit up, walk or carry out a simple routine action using well-worn movement patterns, all without the awareness needed to know it's happening. Whatever the body does under those conditions, it does with virtually no one watching from inside.
